final_answer:
The assistant explains that merge sort operates in three primary steps: dividing, sorting, and merging. First, the algorithm divides the input list into two halves until each sublist contains a single element. Next, it recursively sorts each half. Finally, it merges the sorted sublists back into a single sorted list by comparing elements from each sublist and appending the smaller one to the result. This process ensures a time complexity of O(n log n) in all cases. 

For linked lists, merge sort is preferred over quicksort due to its efficiency in handling pointer-based structures. Quicksort relies on random access to elements and partitioning, which is inefficient for linked lists because accessing elements requires traversing nodes sequentially. Additionally, quicksort's worst-case performance (O(n²)) can occur with already sorted data, whereas merge sort maintains O(n log n) consistency. Merging sorted linked lists is also more efficient, as it only requires adjusting pointers without copying data, reducing overhead compared to quicksort's partitioning steps.
